- Nxeon sells domain registration/renewal/DNS (via name.com), plus VPS + game servers. Features: free Let's Encrypt SSL, dedicated-IP option, NVMe, instant deploy, Singapore location, wallet billing, referral/coupons.

Write **25 original posts** on domains/hosting/decision topics with search intent. Mix:
- Domains: how to register a domain, how to choose a domain name, what are nameservers, how DNS works (A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/TXT records explained), how to point a domain at your VPS/server, DNS propagation explained, what is WHOIS privacy, how to transfer a domain, subdomains explained, common TLDs compared (.com vs .io vs .dev vs .gg), set up email DNS (SPF/DKIM/DMARC).
- Hosting decisions & how-tos: how to host a website, connect a domain to WordPress on a VPS, set up a custom domain for a game server, redirect www to apex, free SSL for a custom domain.
- Comparisons/buyer-intent (honest — Nxeon is a new single-node Singapore host): "Nxeon vs [generic big host] — what to consider", "how much does hosting cost", "do I need a dedicated IP", "shared hosting vs VPS for a growing site". Keep comparisons fair and factual; do NOT invent competitor internals or disparage.
Each post: 500–850 words, ORIGINAL and accurate (write it yourself — never copy). Real DNS examples/records in fenced blocks where relevant. Reference Nxeon naturally. Fields per post: keyword `title`, URL-safe `slug` (topic-prefixed, e.g. `how-to-point-a-domain-to-your-vps`, `dns-records-explained`), 140–160 char `seoDescription`, ~160 char `excerpt`, 3–6 `tags`, `category` one of `"Domains"`/`"Hosting"`/`"Guides"`/`"Comparisons"`, a `coverEmoji`, `author:"Nxeon"`, `published:true`, and `publishedAt` via explicit `new Date("2026-0X-XX")` staggered over ~90 days (NOT `Date.now()`).

## OWNED FILE (create ONLY this)
- `prisma/seed-blog-domains.ts` — idempotent seeder upserting ~25 posts by `slug`, console.log the count, then RUN it: `cd /opt/nxeon && npx tsx prisma/seed-blog-domains.ts`.

## HARD RULES
- Touch ONLY `prisma/seed-blog-domains.ts`. Do NOT edit schema/app/other seeds. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `prisma db push/migrate/generate`, or restart services. Do NOT git commit/push. No new deps.
- ORIGINAL content only — never reproduce copyrighted text; write everything yourself. Honest, factual comparisons only — no fabricated competitor claims, no fake stats.
- Unique slugs in a domains/hosting namespace (won't collide with gaming or vps clusters).

## FINAL REPORT
Count written + seeded (confirm tsx succeeded + printed total), the slug list, anything incomplete.

118	## What shared hosting is
119	
120	On shared hosting, hundreds of websites live on one server and split its resources. You get a control panel, someone else manages the operating system, and it's cheap. 122	## What a VPS is
123	
124	A **Virtual Private Server** carves a physical machine into isolated virtual servers, each with guaranteed CPU, RAM and disk. You get **full root access** — install anything, run any stack, tune the OS. It costs a little more and you manage more yourself, but the resources are genuinely yours.

269	## How DNS actually works

    body: `Computers talk to each other using IP addresses — numbers like \`203.0.113.10\`. People prefer names like \`example.com\`. **DNS**, the Domain Name System, is the translation layer between the two. It's often called the phone book of the internet, and it runs billions of times a second without anyone noticing.

## The problem DNS solves

You can't memorise the IP address of every site you visit, and IPs change over time as sites move servers. Names stay constant while the number behind them changes. DNS lets you use a stable, human-friendly name and always reach the right machine.

## The lookup, step by step

2. **It asks a resolver.** Usually your ISP's or a public resolver like \`1.1.1.1\`. The resolver does the legwork.
3. **The resolver asks a root server.** The root doesn't know \`example.com\`, but it knows who handles \`.com\` and points the resolver there.

5. **The resolver asks your nameservers.** These are *authoritative* — they hold your actual records and return the IP in your A record.

Email was designed without built-in authentication, so anyone can *claim* to send as your domain. ## SPF — who's allowed to send

**SPF (Sender Policy Framework)** lists which servers are permitted to send email for your domain. It's a single TXT record:

\`\`\`
Type: TXT
Name: @
Value: "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:mail.example.net ~all"
TTL: 3600
\`\`\`

Breaking it down:

- \`v=spf1\` — this is an SPF record.
- \`include:...\` — authorise these providers' servers (your email host will give you the exact include).
- \`~all\` — soft-fail anything not listed (mark as suspicious). Use \`-all\` for a strict hard-fail once you're confident.

**Rule:** you may only have *one* SPF record per domain. If you use several mail services, combine their includes into a single record.

## DKIM — a cryptographic signature

**DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)** adds a digital signature to every message, which the receiver verifies against a public key you publish in DNS. It proves the mail wasn't tampered with and genuinely came from you.

Your email provider generates a key and gives you a record to publish, usually as a TXT (or CNAME) at a *selector* subdomain:

\`\`\`
Type: TXT
Name: selector1._domainkey
Value: "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIGfMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEB..."
TTL: 3600
\`\`\`

**DMARC** tells receiving servers what to do when a message *fails* SPF and DKIM, and where to send reports. It's a TXT record at a fixed subdomain:

\`\`\`
Type: TXT
Name: _dmarc
Value: "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com"
TTL: 3600
\`\`\`

The key part is the policy:

- \`p=none\` — monitor only; don't act on failures. **Start here** and read the reports.
- \`p=quarantine\` — send failing mail to spam.
- \`p=reject\` — refuse failing mail outright. The strongest anti-spoofing stance.

## What a wildcard record is

A wildcard uses an asterisk (\`*\`) as the name, meaning "any subdomain not matched by a more specific record":

\`\`\`
Type: A
Name: *
Value: 203.0.113.30
TTL: 3600
\`\`\`

With this in place, \`anything.example.com\`, \`another.example.com\` and \`whatever.example.com\` all resolve to \`203.0.113.30\` — without you creating a record for each.

## When wildcards shine

Wildcards are the right tool in a few clear cases:

- **Multi-tenant apps / SaaS.** If every customer gets \`customer.example.com\`, a wildcard sends them all to your app server, which reads the hostname and serves the right tenant. No per-customer DNS edits.
- **Dynamic or user-generated subdomains.** Blogs, stores or profiles that mint subdomains on the fly.
- **Dev and preview environments.** \`*.dev.example.com\` pointing at a box that routes to whatever branch or preview matches.
- **Catch-all convenience.** So a typo'd subdomain still lands somewhere sensible rather than failing.

## Specific records always win

The key rule: **a specific record overrides the wildcard.** The wildcard only applies to names that have *no* record of their own. So you can mix them:

\`\`\`
Type: A
Name: *
Value: 203.0.113.30      # catch-all app server

Type: A
Name: api
Value: 203.0.113.40      # api.example.com goes here instead
\`\`\`
